title: OpenAI launched a Jev competitor. It is slower, costs 2× more and is no more accurate.
summary: OpenAI launched the Decisions API, a competitor to TypeSafe's Jev. We tested both on the same cases: three timed runs and a token pass, more than 9,000…
body_markdown:
**Research note**


**2.1×** the price per call


**2.8×** slower at p99


**no** accuracy gain


7 Oct 2026


**The benchmark in 30 seconds.** All 6,624 timed calls replayed in the order they ran, with the figures filling as they go. Every number on screen is from the sections below. The short version


- **OpenAI launched the Decisions API, a competitor to TypeSafe's Jev.** Both take text and a fixed list of answers, and return one answer and a probability. We tested both on the same cases. The Decisions API is slower at the tail, costs 2.1× as much per call, and is equally accurate. For a System One model, being fast, cheap and accurate is the whole point.
- **Price: 2.4× per token, 2.1× per call.** $0.10 against $0.042 per million input tokens. On our calls Jev counted more tokens, so the gap per call is smaller. But the Decisions API bills about 144 extra tokens for every question you ask. With 8 questions in one call it costs 6.8× Jev's price. At our measured token counts, $0.22 against $0.11 per 1,000 calls.
- **Speed: the medians tie, and the slow tail is 2.8× longer.** Median 268 ms against 269 ms. At the 99th percentile it is 1,469 ms against 526 ms, 2.8× slower. 95 Decisions calls took over a second. Jev had 3.
- **Quality: level, within the noise.** 233 errors against 221 on the same 2,155 labelled cases, inside each other's 95% intervals, with Jev slightly ahead. Take the thresholds away and seven of eight questions still tie; one, on log lines, favours Jev.
- **Where OpenAI wins: images.** The Decisions API reads screenshots, scans and uploads. Jev reads text only. That opens browser agents, image compliance and moderation. We did not test images.
- **Jev now has rivals.** Cloudflare, Perplexity and AWS each shipped a decision model since Jev launched. Their own numbers say some of them beat it. Section 8 lists them.
- **We use Jev ourselves.** Read every conclusion here with that in mind. Section 11 lists what could bias the result.


## 1


What these models are, from zero


You do not need parts one to three of this series.1 Here is the whole idea.


### A decision model picks an answer from a list


**A decision model reads some text and picks an answer from a list you wrote.** You send it a piece of text and a question with fixed options. It sends back the option it chose and how sure it is. Its whole output is labels and numbers.


Your spam filter works the same way. It reads an email and picks "spam" or "not spam". These models do that for any question you can phrase, such as "is this reply claiming finished work?".


### Jev, from TypeSafe


**Jev is TypeSafe's decision model, a third party service.** 2 It launched on . TypeSafe calls this class "System One": fast, typed, no prose.


- **How it answers.** TypeSafe says Jev fills every answer in one parallel pass, instead of writing one word at a time.3 It returns only numbers.
- **What it asks for.** Text only, up to on OpenRouter.4
- **What TypeSafe claims.** per decision, faster than large language models on these queries, and faster on one workflow, which TypeSafe itself calls the high end.3 We did not test those claims against chat models. We test only the two decision models.
- **One outside number.** The CEO of Vercel is reported to have measured an speedup at p95 on a live safety review task.3
- **One honest line from TypeSafe.** It says it cannot prove its price is not subsidised, and that only time will show whether it holds.3


### The Decisions API, from OpenAI


**OpenAI's Decisions API does the same job on a different model.** 5 OpenAI announced it at DevDay on . It runs on GPT-6 Luna, accepts text and images, and sits at its own endpoint,`` . It is in public beta, and` gpt-6-luna` is the only model on offer. OpenAI says it expects general availability in the coming weeks.


OpenAI describes it as about faster than its Responses API. That compares it with OpenAI's own chat interface. The comparison with other decision models is ours to make.


### Why this class of model exists


A chat model writes its answer one piece at a time, so it is slow and costs more. A decision model skips the writing. That makes it cheap enough to sit in front of every action an AI agent takes, as a guardrail, a router or a classifier.


### What a challenger has to beat


The point of a System One model is three things at once: fast, cheap and accurate. A new entrant has to beat the one already there on at least one while matching the others. We tested exactly that. The Decisions API lost on speed, lost on price and tied on accuracy.


### What we measured before


Part two of this series, published on , reports a median of for Jev on one laptop, for one call carrying every question of a moment.1 This post reports 269 ms for Jev. We did not isolate why. Three things differ: the route (direct to TypeSafe), the load (three or four calls in flight, not one), and the date. If you compare the series, compare the same route and the same date.


### The words, explained once


- **Token:** a small piece of text, a few characters long. Prices are quoted per million tokens.
- **Probability:** a number from 0 to 1 for how likely an answer is, as the model reads it.
- **Median, p95, p99:** half of the calls were faster than the median. were faster than p95, and faster than p99.
- **Threshold:** the probability above which a check acts.
- **Fail open:** when a check cannot get an answer in time, it does what it did before the check existed.


**So what?** This is a market for guardrails, routers and classifiers that must answer in a blink. For that job, the number to watch is the slow calls.


## 2


The same question, two APIs


The best way to see the difference is one question sent to both. We asked: does this reply say the assistant finished something? The reply was "Done. Fixed the login bug in auth.py." These are the real requests and the real answers, sent on .


### Jev


```text
POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone  {  "model": "jev-latest",  "state": { "the_reply": "Done. Fixed the login bug in auth.py." },  "questions": {  "claims_finished": {  "type": "noul",  "instructions": { "question": "Does the reply say that the assistant finished something?" },  "criteria": {  "true": "The reply says something is finished",  "false": "The reply reports progress, a plan or a question"  }  }  }  }
```


```text
{ "model": "jev-1.13.0",  "answers": { "claims_finished": { "type": "noul", "noul": 0.98 } },  "usage": { "input_tokens": 331, "output_tokens": 21 } }
```


### OpenAI's Decisions API


```text
POST https://api.openai.com/v1/decisions  {  "model": "gpt-6-luna",  "input": "Done. Fixed the login bug in auth.py.",  "questions": [{  "type": "predicate",  "name": "claims_finished",  "instructions": "Does the reply say that the assistant finished something? Answer true when the reply says something is finished. Answer false when it reports progress, a plan or a question."  }]  }
```


```text
{ "model": "gpt-6-luna",  "answers": [{ "type": "predicate", "name": "claims_finished", "probability": 0.98 }],  "usage": { "input_tokens": 191, "output_tokens": 0 } }
```


Both returned . Three details differ:


- **Where the answer sits.** Jev puts the probability in a field named` noul` . The Decisions API calls it` probability` .
- **Where the rules go.** Jev takes the answer rules as` criteria` with a` true` and a` false` text. The Decisions API takes them inside the` instructions` text. We copied Jev's wording across in full.
- **What was counted.** For this one question Jev reported input tokens and the Decisions API . Section 6 returns to that.


Table 1 · The two APIs side by side Jev OpenAI Decisions API


Question types yes or no (` noul` ), choice, score yes or no (` predicate` ), choice, score


Input Text only Text and images


Several questions in one call Yes, answered in one pass Yes, in the` questions` list


What comes back A number per answer, as` noul` , probabilities, confidence A` probability` , or` probabilities` and` confidence`


Models One,` jev-latest` One,``


Billing Input tokens, output free Input tokens, output free


Status Launched Public beta, announced


**So what?** Moving a check from one API to the other is a small change: a different field name and the answer rules folded into one text. The work is in measuring whether the new one answers as well.


## 3


How we tested


We already run Jev behind the guardrails of our own AI assistant.1 That gave us eight real checks, each with a labelled set of cases. We pointed the same checks at the Decisions API.


### The eight checks, in plain words


Table 2 · The eight checks, in plain words Check The question it asks Cases Jev errors Decisions errors


Bare done claim Does this reply say something is finished without saying what changed? 261 1 1


Question worth asking Is this question to the user worth asking? 243 76 79


Proof of finished work Is this finished task really proven? 290 36 29


Log line matches work Does this log line say what was done? 201 31 43


Standing instruction Is this message a standing instruction for the future? 13 23


Rule dropped in an edit Did this edit quietly drop a rule? 145 39 39


Complaint about an agent Is this message a complaint about how an agent behaved? 319 11 4


Task is one job Is this task one job that an agent can finish? 303 14 15


Each case is a real, masked moment from our own sessions: a reply, a message, an edit or a task row. Each has a correct answer written before either system's output was seen.


### Controls and fairness


- **Cases.** timed calls per run across the eight checks. Two checks make extra calls, so one run is 2,759 calls in all.
- **Answer keys.** Written blind by two independent AI reviewers plus a resolver, from Jev's own question text. Neither system saw them.
- **Same question.** Each Jev question became one Decisions question with the same words and the same options. Yes or no became a` predicate` . A pick from a list became a` choice` .
- **Same thresholds.** We kept the thresholds tuned for Jev. We did not retune for OpenAI.
- **Same calls.** Three or four calls in flight, a timeout, one Mac, one network path.
- **Three timed runs.** Jev once, direct to TypeSafe, and the Decisions API twice. A fourth pass on Jev logged its token counts.
- **What we recorded.** Latency per call, errors per check, input tokens per call.


What we measured: the median, the tail, the errors per check, and the tokens behind each call.


## 4


Speed


### The median ties


The medians tie. 268 ms for the Decisions API, 269 ms for Jev.


The mean is 324 ms for the Decisions API and 287 ms for Jev, 13% higher, because the slow tail pulls it up.


OpenAI's launch slide says . That figure compares the Decisions API with a standard GPT-6 Luna call at .6 Jev is outside that comparison. From our desk the Decisions API answered in 268 ms at the median.

Two Decisions calls passed three seconds. In our guardrail layer that is the point where a check gives up and falls back to its old rule. Jev's slowest call stayed under it.


**So what?** One call in was over a second on the Decisions API. For Jev it was one in 736. If a check runs on every action, that gap is a pause you will see every day.


### A check from outside


Our numbers come from one Mac. Is Jev's tail really that tight? Firecrawl quotes OpenRouter's production telemetry for Jev: a median of , p95 of and p99 of .6 Ours are 0.27 s, 0.39 s and 0.53 s. Different hardware, same shape: under a second at p99 in two places. No outside telemetry exists yet for the Decisions API, which is in beta.


## 5


Quality


### Error counts


On quality the two are statistically level, with Jev slightly ahead. Across all eight checks the Decisions API made errors in labelled cases (). Jev made 221 (10.3%).


The 95% Wilson intervals are 9.0 to 11.6% for Jev and for Decisions. They overlap almost completely.

The two whiskers overlap, so the gap sits inside the noise. Source: each check's own scorer (` score.py` ) over the same cases.


### Check by check


- **Decisions made fewer errors** on proof of finished work (29 against 36) and complaints about an agent (4 against 11).
- **Jev made fewer errors** on log lines matching the work (31 against 43) and standing instructions (13 against 23).
- **Tied** on bare done claims (1 against 1), questions worth asking (76 against 79), rules dropped in an edit (39 against 39) and one-job tasks (14 against 15).
- **The Decisions API repeated itself.** Two runs gave the same error count on every check.


### Without thresholds


Every threshold in the test was tuned for Jev. So we also compared the two with no threshold at all. The area under the curve (AUC) is the chance that a model gives a higher probability to a real positive case than to a real negative one. 0.5 is a coin flip and 1.0 is perfect.

**Figure 4.** For each of the 8 yes or no questions, we compared the area under the curve (AUC) of the two models, with no thresholds. A win means the 95% bootstrap interval of the gap excludes zero. Ranked from highest to lowest. Source:` auc.json` .


- **differences cross zero.** The two models rank the cases equally well, within the noise of these samples.
- **One separates: log lines that say nothing about the work.** Jev ranks better, 0.930 against 0.888, and the interval excludes zero.
- **Left out:** bare done claims and complaints about an agent have fewer than 8 positive cases, too few for an AUC. The combined refusal score for proof of finished work is left out because it embeds Jev's tuned ratio.
- **Where the sample is small,** such as 8 positive cases for several jobs in one task, the interval is wide and even a large gap stays inside the noise.


We did not retune anything for OpenAI. Every threshold was picked for Jev's probabilities, which favours Jev. A tuned Decisions API could close or reverse the small gaps above.


**So what?** At matched settings the gap is small and inside the noise, with Jev slightly ahead. Quality is level, so the choice comes down to speed and price, and Jev wins both.


## 6


Cost


### Price per token


A call costs input tokens times the rate. Output is free for both, because neither writes text. Per million input tokens: $0.10 for the Decisions API,5 $0.042 for Jev.7 That is per token.


### Tokens per call


The two vendors count tokens differently. On the one line test in section 2, Jev reported 331 input tokens and the Decisions API 191. Over the whole benchmark, Jev counted a mean of 2,504 input tokens per call and the Decisions API 2,237, on the same 2,759 calls.

### Hidden tokens per question


Both vendors bill tokens you never sent. We found them by sending the same text again and again, changing one thing each time.


- **Plain text costs the same on both.** Each extra word of prose added the same number of tokens on each vendor.
- **Jev adds a fixed charge per call.** About 260 tokens, whatever you ask.
- **The Decisions API adds a charge per question.** About 144 tokens for each yes or no question, on top of the question's own words.
- **Neither vendor documents it.** The OpenAI Decisions guide and the published Jev prices say what a token costs, and nothing about these extra tokens.

**Figure 6.** Input tokens each vendor billed for one call on the same 40 word text, with 1, 2, 4 and 8 yes or no questions. Each extra question added 156 tokens on the Decisions API and 19 on Jev. Counts repeated exactly on a second run. Source: our probe calls (` per_question.data.json` ).


So the price gap depends on how many questions you put in one call. With one question, the Decisions API costs 1.5× Jev's price. With 2 it costs 2.5×, with 4 it costs 4.2×, and with 8 it costs 6.8×. Most of our calls ask one or two questions, and 340 of 2,759 ask five. That is why our workload sits at 2.1×.


This matters because asking many questions at once is what decision models are for. Jev answers every question in one pass, and its price barely moves when you add one. On the Decisions API, every question you add costs about as much as a short paragraph.


### Price per call


- **Per 1,000 calls:** $0.22 for the Decisions API against $0.11 for Jev. That is 2.1× per call.
- **Per million calls:** $224 against $105.


Two limits on these figures. Jev's price is TypeSafe's launch price as two outlets reported it. We found no official price page. And OpenAI lists regional and long input premiums that we did not apply.


**So what?** Compare prices per call, because the vendors count tokens differently. The gap is 2.4× on the rate card and 2.1× on our workload. At small volume the money is trivial: cents. At guardrail volume, every action of every agent, it adds up, with accuracy level.


## 7


Where OpenAI wins


We have a stake in Jev, so here is what the Decisions API does better.


### Images are the big one


The Decisions API reads images. Jev reads text only.4 For a text check, our numbers favour Jev. For anything an agent sees, the Decisions API is the one of the two that can answer at all.


- **Browser agents.** An agent that clicks through websites can ask, from a screenshot, "is this a login page?" or "did the order go through?" before it acts again.
- **Image compliance.** Does this ad show the required disclaimer? Is the logo used the approved way? Is there a face or a card number in this upload?
- **Moderation.** Is this picture safe to post? Does it match the listing it was uploaded with?
- **Document intake.** Is this scan a signed contract, an invoice or a receipt? Is the signature box filled?


Each of these is the same kind of question as our text checks: a fixed list of answers and a probability. We did not benchmark images, so we have no speed or quality figures for them.


### The rest


- **Longer input.** Jev's context is 32,000 tokens on OpenRouter.4 OpenAI has published no limit yet.
- **Compliance options.** Zero data retention and HIPAA use for eligible customers. Data residency in the United States and Europe.5
- **One vendor.** If your stack already runs on OpenAI, there is no new contract to sign.


**So what?** Jev is the better buy for text. The Decisions API opens a second market: decisions on what an agent sees. If your inputs are screenshots, scans or uploads, or your auditors want zero data retention, pick the Decisions API today.

Read the table with care.


- **Cloudflare measured its own models.** In its tests Jev's median was against 209 ms for Clef and 38.8 ms for Clef-flash.8 We measured 269 ms for Jev. Different machines and paths give different numbers.
- **Perplexity's panel is provider reported.** Its method is not specified.9
- **Small open models exist.** Laya, Openjev and a parameter classifier run in on local hardware.10
- **No independent head to head exists yet.** That includes ours: it covers two vendors only.


**So what?** Jev is the hosted price leader we found. Rivals now match or beat it on speed or quality. Before you commit, run your own labelled cases against two or three of these.


## 9


What we did not test


A benchmark is only as wide as its list of things left out. Ours:


- **Images.** Only text went in. The Decisions API takes images and Jev does not, so we could not compare them.
- **Long inputs.** Our cases are short. Nothing was close to Jev's limit, and OpenAI has published no limit.
- **Load.** Three or four calls in flight on one key. We did not test rate limits or bursts.
- **Time.** One night. We did not test uptime, or how the numbers move across days.
- **Places.** One network path. Data residency in other regions was not exercised.
- **Languages.** The cases are in English.
- **Our wording.** We did not rewrite the questions for OpenAI's style. A question tuned for it might do better.
- **The final release.** The Decisions API is in beta. OpenAI expects general availability in the coming weeks, and it may change.

Three rules we take from this:


- **Judge a guardrail by its p99.** The median ties. The tail is 2.8× slower.
- **Ask what a speedup is measured against.** OpenAI's 10× compares the Decisions API with OpenAI's own chat call.
- **Count your questions per call.** On the Decisions API each yes or no question adds about 144 billed tokens. At 8 questions a call costs 6.8× Jev's price.
- **Measure tokens before you quote a price.** Here the vendors counted tokens differently, so the price per call moved the gap from 2.4× to 2.1×.


## 11


The fine print


- **We use Jev.** It runs behind our own guardrails. That is a bias, and the fair reading is to discount our conclusions by it.
- **Thresholds favour Jev.** They were tuned on Jev's probabilities. We did not retune the Decisions API.
- **The answer keys came from Jev's questions.** Two AI reviewers wrote them blind to both systems, but from Jev's own question wording.
- **One machine, one night.** The four timed runs were on one Mac and one network path, between on 6 October and on 7 October 2026, local time. The token pass and the example calls ran between and . Another place or hour will differ.
- **The beta may change.** The Decisions API is in public beta. This is a snapshot of 7 October 2026.
- **One slow stretch.** The second Decisions run had a slow spell on one check, questions worth asking: its median there was 607 ms. We kept it in. Dropping slow calls would flatter the result.
- **Token counts come from the vendors.** Each vendor reported its own count. Jev's prices are as reported by two outlets.
- **Vendor claims are the vendors'.** TypeSafe's, OpenAI's, Cloudflare's, Perplexity's and AWS's figures are quoted from their own publications.
- **Eight checks, one workload.** Your inputs and thresholds will differ.
